content: Amylopectin, identified by the CAS number 9037-22-3, is a highly branched polymer composed of glucose molecules and is naturally found in plants. It constitutes one of the two primary components of starch, the other being amylose. Amylopectin is water-soluble and features glucose units connected in a linear arrangement via α(1→4) glycosidic bonds. Branching occurs through α(1→6) glycosidic bonds, which are present approximately every 24 to 30 glucose units. In animals, the structural and compositional counterpart to amylopectin is glycogen. Glycogen, however, exhibits a higher degree of branching, with α(1→6) bonds occurring every 8 to 12 glucose units. Plants store starch, including amylopectin, within specialized organelles known as amyloplasts. When energy is required for cellular processes, plants enzymatically hydrolyze starch, releasing glucose subunits for metabolic use. Humans and other animals that consume plant-based foods possess enzymes capable of hydrolyzing starch into glucose. Starch is composed of approximately 70% amylopectin. Structurally, amylopectin is highly branched and consists of between 2,000 and 200,000 glucose units. Its inner chains are typically composed of 20 to 24 glucose subunits.
